newsitem.title: CROATIA: New Russian order buoys Croatian shipbuilders.
newsitem.headline: New Russian order buoys Croatian shipbuilders.

text.p: An order for ten Russian tankers has brought the order book of Croatia's flagship shipbuilding industry to a bulging $1 billion for the next three years, a far cry from 1993's near-collapse.

Russian shipper Novoship, based in the Black Sea port of Novorosyjsk, is due to sign the tanker order on Monday, bringing to 40 the list of ships on order, the head of Croatian Shipbuilding Ante Baocic told Reuters.

Croatian Shipbuilding is the government agency for supervising the overhaul of the five leading Croatian shipyards. The larger ones will eventually be privatised, and government subsidies made more transparent.
"The Russian order will mean our shipyards are operating at an optimal capacity of some 75 percent well into 2000," Baocic said.

The five big shipyards -- Pula, Rijeka, Kraljevica, Split and Trogir -- had a joint turnover of $430 million in 1996, 10 percent of the country's export earnings, and making Croatia the world's 11th largest shipbuilder.
But the cost of keeping the industry up and running is considerable, Baocic said, putting the cost of subsidies at between five and 10 percent of the turnover.
"There is no country in the world that does not subsidise its shipbuilding. There are obvious interests for Croatia to want to keep the industry," he said.

"Croatian shipbuilding has a well-known label on the world market, it is a labour-intensive industry and brings the state large revenues through taxes, and it is a pivot around which a lot of small firms in the region revolve."
At the peak of the war in former Yugoslavia in 1993, the industry came close to being shut down completely due to financial difficulties and lack of orders.
But government resolve to save it and an earlier order by Russian shipper Novoship for 12 tankers -- the last of which was delivered last month -- worth $370 million, have secured survival.

The radical restructuring programme, launched in 1995, is in full swing and some 3,500 workers out of more than 15,000 currently employed in the five shipyards, will be laid off by the end of the summer, Baocic said.
The next step is selling non-core assets -- smaller parts of firms that used to work on equipping ships -- which are not fully employed any more.
Once the overhaul is complete, the shipyards will undergo technological improvement including computerisation which Baocic said would cost between $1 million and $1.2 million per shipyard.

"In the long term, the goal is to have the shipyards up and running as limited liability companies, to make government subsidies fully transparent and to gradually privatise the bigger ones," Baocic said.
The sell off of at least one yard would improve the performance of the others and the merger of some of them in the near future is likely, he added.
An obvious scenario is for Trogir and Split, which are only 20 kilometres apart, to merge and for Rijeka and Kraljevica, also situated close to one another, to do the same.
